title: Rethinking Retrieval Practice: Remembering Is Not Knowing
author: Carl Hendrick
summary: Hendrick argues that retrieval practice is being misapplied in classrooms as a general-purpose solvent for learning, when it is best understood as a tool for maintaining and stabilising knowledge rather than creating meaningful understanding. He grounds the argument in Gilbert Ryle's distinction between knowing-that and knowing-how and in a Dutch study where pupils who practised retrieving verb-spelling rules recalled them twice as well yet spelled the verbs no better than a worked-examples group. Using Koedinger's KLI framework, he separates memory from induction and explains the gap through a fluency threshold: a rule that is not yet automatic consumes the working memory application needs. A second study on semantic relatedness suggests the testing benefit is smallest where knowledge is already richly connected, which leads him to contrast knowledge-thin and knowledge-rich curricula. He draws four implications: the criterial task, sequence, dosage and curricular architecture all matter. He concludes that education stops too early when it measures what is easy to measure, mistaking recitation of a rule for the ability to deploy it.
points: In the Dutch verb-spelling study, retrieval practice roughly doubled rule recall (about 88 vs 43 per cent) but produced no advantage on actually spelling verbs in sentences.
Memory and induction are separable processes that fail independently, so treating every application failure as a memory problem leads teachers to reach for the wrong tool.
Practising rule recall builds rule recall; fluent application only comes from practising application, ideally to automaticity so it frees working memory.

Retrieval practice yields its largest marginal benefit for isolated, weakly connected material, so quizzes look most 'transformational' in knowledge-thin curricula and more modest where the curriculum already builds semantic webs.
Much learning-science research runs at doses (e.g. three sessions in a week) far below what real skill acquisition needs, which may distort its findings.
quotes: A child who can recite the rules of chess is not thereby a chess player; a child who can describe the strokes of swimming is not thereby a swimmer. Knowing that and knowing how are separable epistemic achievements.

The temptation, especially when we are under pressure to demonstrate impact, is to treat both as memory problems and to reach for the same tool. The error is not to underestimate memory. Memory matters enormously. The error is to treat memory as enough.

This is why fluency is not optional. The point of practising a rule to the point of automaticity is not aesthetic, and it is certainly not antiIintellectual. It is that a rule which cannot be applied without effort cannot be applied at all, once the other cognitive demands arrive.

The quiz in the second curriculum looks less heroic because much of the work is being done elsewhere. The quiz in the first curriculum looks essential, because there is nothing else propping the word up.

The first is that the criterial task matters. If you want pupils to apply a rule fluently, you must eventually practise applying the rule fluently; it is not enough to practise just remembering what the rule is.
The error in the field, if there has been one, has been to treat retrieval practice as though it were a generalIpurpose solvent for the whole of learning. It isn’t.
The child who knows the rule and still writes the wrong form is not failing. She is telling us, with the precision of a diagnostic instrument, that we stopped too early.
